target: AG1’s claim that existing alternative-energy technologies can practically replace fossil fuels.
objection: AG2 argues that renewables and nuclear have not historically supplied enough total U.S. energy—historically never more than 20%—to count as an effective replacement for fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels on a realistic timeline for large countries.
objection: AG2 objects that renewables will not meet the energy needs of large countries anytime soon, so they cannot replace fossil fuels quickly enough to be considered effective in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear energy can help make alternative energies a serious fossil-fuel replacement.
objection: AG2 says nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious climate solution, because accidents such as Fukushima can shut down capacity and wipe out gains in carbon-free electricity.

target: AG2’s use of low historical U.S. alternative-energy share as proof that replacement is impossible.
objection: AG1 objects that low historical penetration of alternative energy in the U.S. does not show replacement is impossible, because past low shares can be explained by fossil-fuel lock-in and slower deployment rather than by any fundamental inability to replace fossil fuels.

target: AG2’s claim that alternative energies cannot provide reliable electricity at the scale needed to replace fossil fuels.
objection: AG1 argues that renewables and nuclear can supply electricity and other energy services reliably enough for large-scale fossil displacement, including firm low-carbon power from nuclear.

target: AG1’s assumption that alternative energies can supply the firm electricity needed for large-scale fossil displacement.
objection: AG2 counters that wind and solar are variable, so low-output periods require dispatchable firm backup rather than relying on variable generation alone, and nuclear is not interruption-proof because it can suffer major disruptions like Fukushima-type shutdowns.

target: AG1’s reduction of fossil-fuel replacement to replacing fossil-fired electricity generation.
objection: AG2 objects that fossil fuels are also used for transportation fuels and industrial heat, so replacing only electricity is not enough to count as replacing fossil fuels overall.

target: AG2’s claim that variable renewables and nuclear cannot reliably supply firm electricity.
objection: AG1 replies that diversified low-carbon systems can provide firm reliability by combining dispatchable renewables, storage, grid flexibility, and dispatchable nuclear, so the reliability objection is not decisive.

target: AG2’s claim that fossil-fuel replacement requires more than electricity generation because of non-electric energy uses.
objection: AG1 objects that many transportation and heating uses can be electrified with EVs and heat pumps, and harder-to-electrify uses can be supplied with low-carbon fuels made from electricity, so replacement is not blocked by non-electric end uses.

target: AG1’s claim that low-carbon electricity can be converted into synthetic fuels and heat for hard-to-electrify sectors.
objection: AG2 argues that electricity-to-fuels conversion is energy-inefficient, so replacing fossil fuels this way would require much more low-carbon electricity generation than AG1 acknowledges.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can scale fast enough to supply the surplus electricity and industrial capacity needed for hard-to-electrify sectors.
objection: AG2 says large countries demand far more energy than alternative electricity can provide soon, so there will not be enough surplus low-carbon power to support large-scale fuel conversion and industrial retrofits in the near term.

target: AG2’s claim that electricity-to-fuels conversion makes hard-to-electrify sectors an insurmountable barrier.
objection: AG1 responds that fossil-fuel services do not all need to be replaced by synthetic liquids or gases, because large portions of transport and building heat can be directly electrified, while the remaining hard-to-electrify uses can be handled through electricity-derived fuels and heat.

target: AG1’s claim that hard-to-electrify fossil uses can be covered by low-carbon fuels made from electricity.
objection: AG2 reiterates that conversion to chemical fuels is inefficient and would require an unrealistically large surplus of low-carbon electricity on a large-country timeline, so the conversion route cannot scale to fully replace fossil demand quickly.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can meet continuous demand reliably enough to replace fossil fuels.
objection: AG2 argues that effective replacement requires continuous reliability comparable to fossil fuels, but wind and solar have extended low-output periods and present long-duration storage is not available at the needed national scale to cover them.

target: AG2’s claim that long-duration storage shortages make alternative energy unable to replace fossil fuels.
objection: AG1 says dispatchable low-carbon nuclear can provide the needed reliability during extended low-wind and low-solar periods, so the storage problem is not an absolute barrier once nuclear is included.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as interruption-proof firm power.
objection: AG2 objects that nuclear plants still have planned outages and unplanned failures, so nuclear cannot be treated as an always-available substitute that eliminates all generation gaps.

target: AG1’s inference from nuclear outages to the conclusion that fossil backup is unnecessary.
objection: AG2 argues that if nuclear can still leave gaps during low-renewable periods, then a renewables-plus-nuclear system still needs additional dispatchable backup, realistically supplied by natural gas.

target: AG2’s inference that nuclear outages necessarily require fossil backup.
objection: AG1 counters that power systems use reserves and redundancy so individual generator outages do not force reliance on continuous fossil backup, and high-renewable countries show that low-carbon systems can remain reliable at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear’s quick deployment and low land use remove the need for a fossil bridge.
objection: AG2’s bridge-fuel argument assumes alternatives cannot scale firm low-carbon capacity fast enough, so nuclear’s advantages do not by themselves eliminate the need for natural gas during the transition.

target: AG2’s claim that a temporary fossil bridge means alternatives cannot effectively replace fossil fuels.
objection: AG1 argues that a temporary fossil-fuel bridge during scale-up is compatible with effective long-run replacement, because the relevant standard is ending fossil dependence over the long run rather than having zero fossil use during the build-out period.

target: AG2’s claim that natural gas is necessary because variable renewables need a dispatchable bridge.
objection: AG1 objects that firm low-carbon renewable sources such as hydropower and geothermal can cover low-wind and low-solar periods, so natural gas is not intrinsically required as a permanent dispatchable bridge.
